definition: Feeling or showing pleasure or contentment.
example: She was happy to finally be home.

synonyms.definition: Full of great happiness.
Noticeably happy and optimistic.
Peacefully satisfied with what one has.
Pleased and delighted about something.

antonyms.definition: Feeling or showing sorrow.
Wretchedly unhappy or uncomfortable.
Depressed, without hope or cheer.
Feeling or showing deep grief.

distractors.definition: Having good things happen by chance.
distractors.note: Luck often makes people happy, but lucky describes fortune, not feeling.

distractors.definition: Very enthusiastic and eager; stirred up.
distractors.note: Excitement is high energy and can be nervous or anxious, not necessarily happy.

distractors.definition: Not showing nervousness, anger or strong emotion.
distractors.note: You can be calm and unhappy; calm is about agitation, not pleasure.

definition: Ready to face and endure danger or pain; showing courage.
example: The brave firefighter went back in for the dog.

synonyms.definition: Not deterred by danger or pain.
Willing to take risks; confident and daring.
Showing courage or determination, often heroically.
Lacking fear.

antonyms.definition: Lacking courage in facing danger.
Showing a lack of courage or confidence; easily frightened.
Feeling afraid; showing fear or anxiety.

distractors.definition: Heedless of danger or the consequences of one's actions.
distractors.note: Reckless ignores danger; brave faces danger knowingly. Bravery is a virtue, recklessness isn't.

distractors.definition: Having physical power or great force.
distractors.note: Strength is power; bravery is willingness to face fear.

distractors.definition: Feeling satisfaction in one's achievements, or having too high an opinion of oneself.
distractors.note: Pride is about self-regard, not courage.

definition: Very large in size, quantity or extent.
example: An enormous wave crashed over the pier.

synonyms.definition: Extremely large.
Extremely large or great, especially in scale.
Of very great extent, especially in area.
Extremely large, like a colossus (a giant statue).

antonyms.definition: Very small.
Extremely small.
(my-NOOT) Extremely small.

distractors.definition: Of great weight.
distractors.note: Something can be small and heavy (a gold bar) or huge and light (a balloon).

distractors.definition: Great in number; many.
distractors.note: Numerous counts things; enormous measures size.

distractors.definition: Of great height.
distractors.note: Tall is only about height; enormous covers overall size.

definition: Existing or available in large quantities; more than enough.
example: Fresh water is abundant in the region.

synonyms.definition: Existing in great quantities.
Enough or more than enough.
Abundant in supply or quantity.
Exuberantly plentiful; abundant (often of flow).

antonyms.definition: Insufficient for the demand; in short supply.
Thinly scattered or distributed.
Lacking in quantity or quality; barely enough.

distractors.definition: Costing a lot of money.
distractors.note: Price isn't quantity — in fact, abundant things are usually cheap.

distractors.definition: Happening often.
distractors.note: Frequent is about how often something occurs, not how much of it exists.

distractors.definition: Able to produce abundant crops or offspring.
distractors.note: Fertile land produces abundance; it isn't the abundance itself.

definition: Free of deceit; truthful and sincere.
example: Give me your honest opinion.

synonyms.definition: Telling or expressing the truth.
Free from pretence; genuine.
Truthful and straightforward, even when it's uncomfortable.
Open, honest and direct in speech.

antonyms.definition: Guilty of or involving deception.
Behaving or prone to behave untruthfully.
Using underhanded tactics to achieve goals.

distractors.definition: Having good manners; respectful.
distractors.note: Politeness sometimes means softening the truth — the opposite of being candid.

distractors.definition: Unassuming about one's abilities or achievements.
distractors.note: Modesty is about not boasting, not about telling the truth.

distractors.definition: Giving firm and constant support to a person or cause.
distractors.note: Loyalty is faithfulness; a loyal friend might still lie for you.

definition: Having or showing care and steady effort in one's work or duties.
example: A diligent student reviews her notes every evening.

synonyms.definition: Tending to work with energy and commitment.
Constantly and energetically busy at work.
Showing great care, attention and persistence.
Wishing to do one's work or duty well and thoroughly.

antonyms.definition: Unwilling to work or use energy.
Avoiding work; not active.
Failing to take proper care in doing something.

distractors.definition: Having a high capacity for thinking and learning.
distractors.note: Ability isn't effort — a brilliant person can be lazy.

distractors.definition: Happening or doing something at the agreed time.
distractors.note: Being on time is one habit; diligence is sustained careful effort.

distractors.definition: Having a strong desire for success.
distractors.note: Ambition is wanting; diligence is doing the steady work.

definition: Belonging to the very distant past; very old.
example: They walked among the ruins of an ancient city.

synonyms.definition: Having lived or existed for a long time.
Very old or old-fashioned; belonging to an earlier period.
Old and valuable because of age (of objects).
Having existed for a very long time.

antonyms.definition: Relating to the present or recent times.
Not existing before; recently made or discovered.
Belonging to or occurring in the present.

distractors.definition: Worth a great deal of money or highly useful.
distractors.note: Many ancient things are valuable, but value and age are different properties.

distractors.definition: Known about by many people.
distractors.note: Fame has nothing to do with age.

distractors.definition: Easily broken or damaged.
distractors.note: Old objects are often fragile, but fragile describes strength, not age.

definition: Showing readiness to give more of something, like money or time, than expected.
example: It was generous of you to drive us all the way.

synonyms.definition: Giving freely to those in need; kind in judging others.
Very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival.
Giving generously; also, large in quantity.
Larger or more generous than is usual.

antonyms.definition: Unwilling to give or spend; ungenerous.
Hoarding wealth and spending as little as possible.
Extremely unwilling to spend money.

distractors.definition: Having a great deal of money.
distractors.note: Having money is not the same as giving it.

distractors.definition: Kind and pleasant.
distractors.note: Friendliness is warmth; generosity is giving.

distractors.definition: Feeling thankful.
distractors.note: Gratitude is how you feel about receiving, not giving.

definition: Not showing or feeling nervousness, anger or other strong emotion; still.
example: She stayed calm when the alarm went off.

synonyms.definition: Free from disturbance; peaceful.
Calm, peaceful and untroubled.
Not easily upset or excited; calm.
Free from disturbance; quiet and calm.

antonyms.definition: Feeling or appearing troubled or nervous.
Experiencing worry or unease.
Characterized by conflict, disorder or confusion; not still.

distractors.definition: Needing or ready for sleep.
distractors.note: Tired isn't the same as untroubled — you can be sleepy and anxious.

distractors.definition: Of low temperature; or lacking warmth of feeling.
distractors.note: A cold person is unfriendly, not necessarily calm.

distractors.definition: Able to wait or tolerate delays without getting upset.
distractors.note: Close, but patience is about tolerating delay or difficulty; calm is a general state.

definition: Needing much effort or skill to accomplish, deal with or understand.
example: The final exam was difficult but fair.

synonyms.definition: Requiring a great deal of effort.
Involving strenuous effort; tiring.
Testing one's abilities; demanding.
Requiring much skill or effort.

antonyms.definition: Achieved without great effort.
Easily understood or done.
Requiring no physical or mental exertion.

distractors.definition: Able or likely to cause harm.
distractors.note: A task can be easy but dangerous, or hard but safe.

distractors.definition: Of considerable or unusual length.
distractors.note: Long isn't necessarily hard.

distractors.definition: Causing physical or emotional pain.
distractors.note: Pain and difficulty often travel together, but they aren't the same.

definition: Not discovered or known about; little known. (Here: the "not famous" sense.)
example: The song was written by an obscure poet from Galway.

synonyms.definition: Not known or familiar.
Not widely known.
Not celebrated or praised as it deserves.
Not previously announced, expected or praised.

antonyms.definition: Known about by many people.
Known and admired by many.
Greatly admired; famous.
Important; famous; standing out.

distractors.definition: With no special or distinctive features.
distractors.note: Something can be remarkable but obscure — just undiscovered.

distractors.definition: Belonging to the very distant past.
distractors.note: Many ancient things are very famous (the pyramids).

distractors.definition: Kept from being known by others on purpose.
distractors.note: Secret is deliberately hidden; obscure simply isn't widely known.

definition: Strongly wanting to do or have something.
example: The puppy was eager to go outside.

synonyms.definition: Having or showing eagerness or enthusiasm.
Having intense and eager enjoyment or interest.
Having a keen interest in or enthusiasm for something.
Having great energy or enthusiasm for a cause or objective.

antonyms.definition: Unwilling and hesitant.
Not ready, eager or prepared to do something.
Showing no interest, enthusiasm or concern.
Having no particular interest or sympathy.

distractors.definition: Restless and unable to wait calmly.
distractors.note: Eagerness can cause impatience, but impatience is about waiting, and can come with irritation.

distractors.definition: Feeling a need for food.
distractors.note: Used figuratively ("hungry for success") it's close — but literally it's about food.

distractors.definition: Easily agitated or alarmed; anxious.
distractors.note: Nerves are anxiety, not desire.

definition: Easily broken or damaged; delicate.
example: Pack the fragile glasses in newspaper.

synonyms.definition: Easily broken or damaged; fine in texture.
Hard but liable to break or shatter easily.
Capable of being broken.
Weak and delicate, especially of a person.

antonyms.definition: Strongly and solidly built.
Strong and healthy; not easily broken.
Able to withstand wear, pressure or damage.

distractors.definition: Of little weight.
distractors.note: Light things can be tough (a feather, plastic); weight and strength differ.

distractors.definition: Allowing light to pass through so you can see behind.
distractors.note: Glass is both, but bulletproof glass is transparent and far from fragile.

distractors.definition: Costing a lot of money.
distractors.note: Price doesn't tell you how breakable something is.

definition: To express warm approval or admiration of someone or something.
example: Critics praised the film's performances.

synonyms.definition: To praise formally or officially.
To show strong approval of; literally, to clap.
To praise highly, especially in public.
To praise enthusiastically and publicly.

antonyms.definition: To indicate the faults of someone or something disapprovingly.
To express complete disapproval of.
To express severe, often formal, disapproval.
To represent as being of little worth; belittle.

distractors.definition: To express gratitude to someone.
distractors.note: Thanks acknowledges a favour; praise judges something as good.

distractors.definition: To give support, confidence or hope.
distractors.note: Encouragement looks forward ("you can do it"); praise looks at what was done.

distractors.definition: To praise excessively or insincerely.
distractors.note: The trap! Flattery is praise that isn't sincere, often to gain favour — not a neutral synonym.

definition: To start; to perform the first part of an action.
example: The concert will begin at eight.

synonyms.definition: To begin doing or happening.
To begin (formal).
To cause a process or action to begin.
To start or set in motion an activity or enterprise.

antonyms.definition: To come or bring to a final point.
To bring a task or activity to an end.
To bring something to an end (formal).
To come to an end; stop.

distractors.definition: To make ready for use or an event.
distractors.note: Preparing happens before beginning.

distractors.definition: To keep going without stopping.
distractors.note: Continuing is the middle — after beginning, before ending.

distractors.definition: To make an effort to do something.
distractors.note: You can begin without trying hard, and try without beginning anything new.

definition: To become or make greater in size, amount, intensity or degree.
example: Ticket prices will increase next year.

synonyms.definition: To become larger or greater over time.
To become or make larger or more extensive.
To make something greater by adding to it.
To increase rapidly in intensity or seriousness.

antonyms.definition: To make or become smaller or fewer.
To make smaller or less in amount or size.
To make or become less.
To become or make smaller in size or amount.

distractors.definition: To make or become better.
distractors.note: More isn't always better — increasing pollution doesn't improve anything.

distractors.definition: To say or do again.
distractors.note: Doing something again doesn't make it larger.

distractors.definition: To begin to move or happen more quickly.
distractors.note: Close, but it's specifically an increase in speed, not in size or amount.

definition: Having or showing experience, knowledge and good judgement.
example: It was a wise decision to leave early.

synonyms.definition: Having keen mental discernment and good judgement.
Having, showing or done with good judgement.
Acting with care and thought for the future.
Able to accurately assess situations and turn them to one's advantage.

antonyms.definition: Lacking good sense or judgement.
Not sensible; foolish.
Not showing care for the consequences of an action.
Acting without careful consideration of the consequences.

distractors.definition: Having received a good education.
distractors.note: Knowledge isn't judgement: plenty of educated people make unwise choices.

distractors.definition: Having lived for a long time.
distractors.note: Age can bring wisdom, but they're different things.

distractors.definition: Solemn or thoughtful in character.
distractors.note: Looking thoughtful isn't the same as judging well.

definition: Unfriendly; antagonistic; showing or feeling opposition.
example: The crowd grew hostile when the match was delayed.

synonyms.definition: Showing active opposition or hostility.
Not friendly or kind.
Hostile and aggressive; eager to fight.
Involving or characterized by conflict or opposition.

antonyms.definition: Kind and pleasant.
Characterized by friendliness and absence of discord.
Warm and friendly.
Behaving in a polite or friendly way to a guest or newcomer.

distractors.definition: From or relating to another country.
distractors.note: Unfamiliar isn't the same as unfriendly.

distractors.definition: Demanding that rules be obeyed.
distractors.note: A strict teacher can still be warm and on your side.

distractors.definition: Producing much noise.
distractors.note: Volume isn't attitude: a cheering crowd is loud and friendly.

definition: Of short duration, or using few words.
example: After a brief pause, she continued speaking.

synonyms.definition: Lasting a small amount of time.
Giving a lot of information clearly in few words.
Briefly and clearly expressed.
Lasting for a very short time.

antonyms.definition: Lasting or taking a great amount of time.
Of considerable or unusual length, sometimes tediously so.
Continuing for a long time or longer than usual.
Lasting longer than expected or than usual.

distractors.definition: Easily understood or done.
distractors.note: A short message can still be complicated.

distractors.definition: Occurring quickly and unexpectedly.
distractors.note: Sudden is about how it starts; brief is about how long it lasts.

distractors.definition: Of a size less than normal.
distractors.note: Small measures size; brief measures time or length of speech.

definition: With no special or distinctive features; normal.
example: It started as an ordinary Tuesday morning.

synonyms.definition: Occurring, found or done often; not unusual.
Habitually or typically occurring or done.
Having the distinctive qualities of a particular type.
Happening or used every day; commonplace.

antonyms.definition: Very unusual or remarkable.
Worthy of attention; striking.
Unusual; not typical, often unusually good.
Not habitually or commonly occurring or done.

distractors.definition: Not interesting; tedious.
distractors.note: Ordinary things can be delightful. Boring is a judgement; ordinary is a description.

distractors.definition: Low in price.
distractors.note: Price isn't the point — an ordinary car can be expensive.

distractors.definition: Liked or admired by many people.
distractors.note: Being liked isn't the same as being common.

definition: To make something previously unknown or hidden known or seen.
example: The magician finally revealed how the trick worked.

synonyms.definition: To make information known, especially something secret.
To make known private or sensitive information.
To make visible by uncovering; to reveal something wrong.
To remove a covering from; to show publicly for the first time.

antonyms.definition: To keep from sight; hide.
To put or keep out of sight.
To refuse to give something that is due or wanted.

distractors.definition: To find something unexpectedly or during a search.
distractors.note: Discovering is finding out yourself; revealing is showing it to others.

distractors.definition: To make an idea clear by describing it in detail.
distractors.note: You can explain something everyone already knows. Revealing requires it to have been hidden.

distractors.definition: To give an account in words of someone or something.
distractors.note: Describing gives detail; it doesn't imply anything was hidden.

definition: Sparing or economical with money or food; avoiding waste.
example: A frugal lifestyle helped them save for a house.

synonyms.definition: Using money and resources carefully and not wastefully.
Giving good value for the money or effort; careful not to waste.
Moderate; economical; using little.

antonyms.definition: Lacking restraint in spending money or using resources.
Using or expending something carelessly or needlessly.
Sumptuously rich or elaborate; spending freely.
Recklessly extravagant or wasteful.

distractors.definition: Lacking enough money to live comfortably.
distractors.note: Frugality is a choice; a wealthy person can be frugal and a poor one wasteful.

distractors.definition: Having an excessive desire for more, especially money.
distractors.note: Greed is wanting more; frugality is using less.

distractors.definition: Unwilling to give or spend; ungenerous.
distractors.note: The trap! Stingy is negative — refusing to share. Frugal is a positive habit of not wasting.

definition: Hopeful and confident about the future.
example: Doctors are optimistic about her recovery.

synonyms.definition: Feeling or inspiring hope.
Constructive and confident; focusing on the good.
Cheerfully optimistic, especially in a bad situation.
Cheerful and optimistic (informal).

antonyms.definition: Tending to see the worst aspect of things.
Showing the loss of all hope.
Expecting or accepting failure too readily.

distractors.definition: Having a sensible, practical idea of what can be achieved.
distractors.note: Realism can be optimistic or pessimistic depending on the facts.

distractors.definition: Feeling or showing pleasure.
distractors.note: Happiness is about now; optimism is about the future.

distractors.definition: Feeling sure about oneself or one's abilities.
distractors.note: Close, but confidence is about yourself; optimism is about how things will turn out.

definition: Producing strong, clear images in the mind; of colour, intensely bright.
example: I have a vivid memory of my first day at school.

synonyms.definition: Full of energy and life; bright and striking.
Very bright or radiant.
Attracting attention by being unusual or prominent.
Clear and detailed, often uncomfortably so.

antonyms.definition: Lacking brightness, interest or excitement.
Lacking brightness or interest; dreary.
Having lost colour or brightness; dimmed.
Vague, indistinct or ill-defined.

distractors.definition: Producing much noise.
distractors.note: "Loud colours" is a figure of speech; loud is mostly about sound.

distractors.definition: Correct in all details; exact.
distractors.note: A vivid memory can be completely wrong — vividness isn't accuracy.

distractors.definition: Having happened not long ago.
distractors.note: Old memories can be vivid and yesterday's can be hazy.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; not having one obvious meaning.
example: The contract's wording was ambiguous, so both sides claimed victory.

synonyms.definition: Open to more than one interpretation, often deliberately.
Not easy to see, hear or understand.
Of uncertain, indefinite or unclear meaning.

antonyms.definition: Not open to more than one interpretation.
Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion.
Clearly defined; precise.
Easy to perceive, understand or interpret.

distractors.definition: Consisting of many interconnecting parts; intricate.
distractors.note: A complicated statement can have exactly one meaning.

distractors.definition: Not according with truth or fact.
distractors.note: Ambiguity is about meaning, not truth: a lie can be perfectly clear.

distractors.definition: Having mixed feelings about something.
distractors.note: The classic mix-up: ambivalent describes a person's feelings; ambiguous describes a message's meaning.
